Why Every Pakistani Business Website Needs SSL (2026): What Free SSL Covers

By ZedgeHost Team · 27 November 2026 · 7 min read

Short answer: yes. Every business website needs an SSL certificate, even if it sells nothing online. Without one, browsers label the site "Not secure", contact forms send visitor details in readable text, and customers trust the business less. A free SSL certificate covers the essentials: it encrypts the connection, turns the address into HTTPS, and shows the padlock visitors expect. At ZedgeHost, free SSL is included in every hosting plan, from the Starter plan at Rs 1,499 per year, so a Pakistani business does not need to pay extra for it.

What an SSL certificate actually does

An SSL certificate is a small data file installed on the server that hosts your website. When a visitor opens your site, their browser checks the certificate first. If it is valid, the browser and the server set up an encrypted connection before a single page is sent. That encrypted connection is what turns http at the start of your address into https.

The certificate does three jobs. First, it encrypts the data that travels between your visitor and your website, so nobody in between can read it. Second, it confirms that the server really belongs to your domain name, because the certificate is only issued after the issuing authority checks that the person asking for it controls the domain. Third, it tells the browser the connection is safe to use, which is why the address bar shows a padlock instead of a warning.

The name SSL is short for Secure Sockets Layer. The current version of the technology is called TLS, but hosting companies and browsers still use the word SSL for the certificate itself. For a business owner, the detail does not matter. What matters is that the certificate is valid, it covers your domain, and it renews on time.

What visitors see without SSL

A website without SSL loads over plain http, and modern browsers say so openly. Chrome and other browsers label the page "Not secure" next to the address. If the certificate is expired or broken, the browser shows a full-page warning instead, and most visitors will not click past it.

That warning matters even for a simple business website. A brochure site with only a contact form still collects names, phone numbers, and email addresses. Without encryption, that information travels in readable text, and anyone on the same public Wi-Fi can potentially see it. A customer who notices the warning has a simple choice: fill in the form anyway, or find a competitor whose site looks safe. Most choose the competitor.

The warning also hurts the business in search. Google has used HTTPS as a ranking signal since 2014. It is a small signal on its own, and it will not rescue a weak website, but there is no reason to give it away. A site that loads over HTTPS also keeps its referral data intact when visitors arrive from other secure sites, so traffic reports stay more accurate.

What free SSL covers

A free SSL certificate encrypts the connection just as strongly as a basic paid one. The encryption is the same. The difference is in the checks that come with the certificate, not in the protection of the data itself. For a typical small business website, a free certificate covers everything the site needs.

  • Encryption. Everything between the visitor and the server is scrambled while it travels, including form submissions, logins, and bookings.
  • HTTPS and the padlock. The site loads over https and shows the padlock in the address bar, so the "Not secure" label goes away.
  • Domain check. The certificate proves the site really belongs to your domain name, which makes simple impersonation harder.
  • Automatic renewal. At ZedgeHost the free certificate renews automatically, so the site does not suddenly show an expired-certificate warning.

What free SSL does not cover

This is the part most guides skip, and it matters. SSL protects data while it travels between the visitor and the server. It does not protect anything else. A site with a valid certificate can still be hacked, and its owner still needs the rest of the security basics.

  • Malware on the website. SSL cannot see or remove malicious code that is already on the site. That needs malware scanning and removal, which is what SiteLock website security is for.
  • Weak passwords. A certificate does nothing if the admin password is guessable or shared. Use a strong, unique password for hosting, WordPress, and email.
  • Outdated plugins and themes. Most WordPress break-ins come through software that was never updated. Keep WordPress, themes, and plugins current, and remove the ones you do not use.
  • Lost data. SSL is not a backup. If the site is deleted or damaged, only a backup brings it back. Weekly backups are included in every ZedgeHost plan.
  • Fake websites pretending to be you. A free certificate only checks control of a domain. A lookalike domain can get its own certificate, so customers should still check the exact address before they pay.

Think of SSL as the lock on the front door. It keeps the conversation private, but it does not fix a broken window, a weak lock on the back door, or a missing spare key. A business website needs SSL plus the basics: strong passwords, updates, backups, and malware scanning.

Free SSL vs paid SSL: when paying makes sense

For most Pakistani small businesses, free SSL is enough. A paid certificate makes sense only in a few specific cases.

Certificate typeWhat it addsWho needs it
Free SSL (Domain Validated)Encryption and HTTPS, issued after a domain control checkBlogs, brochure sites, portfolios, small business sites, and most online stores
Paid SSL (Organisation Validated)Also checks that the company legally existsLarger companies that want visitors to see the organisation behind the site
Paid SSL (Extended Validation)The strictest company checks before issueBanks, financial services, and sites where identity proof is part of the product

A paid certificate does not encrypt data more strongly than a free one. It buys stronger identity checks and, in some cases, a warranty from the issuer. If your business is a small shop, a clinic, a school, or a freelancer portfolio, the free certificate that comes with your hosting is the right choice. Spend the money on backups and malware protection instead.

5 mistakes Pakistani businesses make with SSL

These are the mistakes that turn a working certificate into a warning in the browser.

  • Thinking SSL means the site is fully secure. SSL covers data in transit only. Passwords, updates, backups, and malware scanning still need attention.
  • Leaving mixed content on the page. If a secure page loads even one image, script, or stylesheet over plain http, the browser flags the page. After moving to HTTPS, check that every link on the page uses https too.
  • Securing only the homepage. The certificate must cover the whole site, including www and non-www versions, and every subdomain that serves pages, such as shop or blog.
  • Forgetting renewal. An expired certificate triggers a full-page browser warning, which looks worse than having no certificate at all. Automatic renewal, included with ZedgeHost hosting, removes this risk.
  • Paying for SSL on top of hosting that already includes it. Before buying a certificate anywhere, check what the hosting plan already includes. Every ZedgeHost plan includes free SSL, so a separate purchase would be money spent twice.
